en.title: Peace and Conflict Studies: the whole course
en.short: What peace and conflict studies is, how the degree is organised, the main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Peace and conflict studies is an interdisciplinary field. It studies why conflicts arise, how they escalate, how people and institutions prevent or limit violence, and how societies build lasting peace. It draws on politics, sociology, anthropology, psychology, law, economics, history and philosophy. It is both empirical, asking what happens and why, and normative, asking what should be done. The field distinguishes conflict from violence. Conflict is a disagreement or incompatibility of goals, interests or values; it is not always harmful. Violence includes direct harm, structural injustice and cultural beliefs that justify harm. Peace is often described as negative peace, the absence of direct violence, and positive peace, the presence of justice and conditions for nonviolent change. These definitions are starting points, not final answers.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text: Length, award and curriculum differ by country and institution. Awards include BA, BSc, MA, MSc, MPhil and PhD, and some institutions offer postgraduate diplomas or certificates. In Nigeria, a bachelor’s degree is commonly four years, but entry requirements and programme length vary. Some universities run peace and conflict studies as a full department or programme; others offer it as a specialisation within political science, sociology or international relations. Universities, public and private, are regulated by the National Universities Commission, but each university sets its own curriculum and award title. In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s degree is commonly three years and a taught master’s one year. In South Africa, a bachelor’s degree is commonly three years, followed by an honours year and then a master’s. Always check your own handbook for the current structure, credit load and graduation rules.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually begins with foundations: the history, scope and careers of the field; key concepts of peace, conflict and violence; levels and types of conflict; causes and dynamics; theories of conflict; conflict analysis; histories of peace thought and movements; human rights, justice and peace; and evidence and inquiry. These give you the vocabulary and analytical habits for later work.

The core then covers practice and institutions: conflict prevention and early warning; negotiation; mediation, arbitration and adjudication; dialogue, reconciliation and apology; nonviolence and civil resistance; peacemaking, peacekeeping and ceasefire monitoring; peacebuilding and reconstruction; transitional justice; gender; religion and ethnicity; natural resources and environment; development, security and humanitarian action; disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration; research methods; professional ethics; the African Peace and Security Architecture; and Nigerian conflicts and peacebuilding.

At master’s level, advanced theory deepens the study of conflict and peace. Peacebuilding and statebuilding theory examines external intervention and local ownership. Research methods prepares a dissertation. Peace measurement and impact evaluation teaches you to assess whether programmes work.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study by connecting concepts to cases. For each conflict, map the actors, their interests, the issues, the timeline, the levels involved and the attempts at settlement. Use a simple conflict analysis framework and write short case notes. Keep a glossary of terms and test yourself on definitions. Read primary documents where possible, such as peace agreements, mandates, laws and official reports, and use peer-reviewed sources for analysis.

Practise skills, not only reading. Role-play negotiation and mediation with classmates. Draft a ceasefire checklist, a peacebuilding project outline and a policy brief. Learn basic research methods and how to judge evidence. When you use a statistic, record its date, definition and source. Ask whose voice is missing, especially women, young people, minorities and displaced people. Compare cases across countries, but do not assume that one country’s institutions or history apply everywhere.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include treating conflict as always violent or always bad, and treating peace as only the absence of war. Students often use one theory, such as greed or identity, as a complete explanation. They confuse negotiation with mediation, and mediation with arbitration or adjudication. They treat reconciliation as if it required impunity, or transitional justice as a single policy. They ignore local agency and present outside interveners as the only actors.

Other errors are weak sourcing, undefined terms and normative claims presented as evidence. Students sometimes compare statistics without checking definitions, or generalise from one Nigerian or African case to the whole continent. In practice questions, check the mandate, the consent of the parties and the ethical limits of the role. In essays, state your assumptions and the evidence that would change your conclusion.

keyPoints: Peace and conflict studies examines the causes and dynamics of conflict and the practices that prevent violence and build peace.
Conflict is not the same as violence, and peace is more than the absence of war.
Definitions and theories are tools; no single theory explains every conflict.
Negotiation, mediation, arbitration and adjudication are different processes with different roles.
Always check the date, definition and source of evidence, and name the country and institution a rule belongs to.
Local actors and affected communities are central to peacebuilding, not passive recipients.

en.title: The Field of Peace and Conflict Studies: Origins, Scope and Careers
en.short: How peace and conflict studies began, what it covers, its main debates, and the careers it can lead to.

sections.heading: Origins
sections.text: Peace and conflict studies is an interdisciplinary field: it draws on politics, history, law, sociology, psychology, economics and anthropology. It grew from several roots. These include older peace movements and international relations, and the peace research that developed after the Second World War and during the Cold War, when nuclear war made the study of conflict urgent. Early centres, journals and scholars such as Norway’s Johan Galtung helped make it a recognised academic field. The Journal of Conflict Resolution began in 1957 and the Journal of Peace Research in 1964. Since the 1990s the field has widened from war between states to civil war, peacebuilding, human rights and development.

sections.heading: Scope and debates
sections.text: Its scope runs from the causes of violence to the prevention and settlement of conflict and the building of lasting peace. It studies negotiation, mediation, peacekeeping, reconciliation and justice, but this course treats those topics separately. A key debate is whether the field should be neutral and scientific or openly committed to peace and social justice. Another is whether outside international actors or local communities should lead peace work. Scholars also argue over quantitative and qualitative methods, and over whether 'conflict resolution' or 'peace studies’ best names the field. These debates are healthy: they show that the field is not one single theory.

sections.heading: Study and careers
sections.text:
First-year study covers key concepts, theories, methods and cases. Later you may specialise in mediation, peacebuilding, security, gender or research. Careers are varied and depend on the country and employer. Graduates work in government diplomatic services, civil service, regional bodies such as the African Union and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), the United Nations, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), humanitarian agencies, research institutes and teaching. Many roles need further training, languages, field experience or a master’s degree. Check each employer’s requirements.

Example: Amina, a student in Kano, Nigeria, volunteers with a local peace committee. She writes reports, helps organise dialogue meetings and learns how research and practice connect. That experience can support later applications for NGO or research work.

keyPoints: Peace and conflict studies is interdisciplinary, drawing on politics, history, law, sociology, psychology, economics and anthropology.
It grew from peace movements, international relations and post-Second World War peace research, and expanded after the Cold War.
Its scope covers the causes of conflict, prevention, settlement, peacebuilding, justice and reconciliation.
Key debates concern neutrality versus commitment, local versus international leadership, and quantitative versus qualitative methods.
Careers include diplomacy, civil service, regional organisations, NGOs, humanitarian work, research and teaching.
Requirements vary by country and employer, so check current official information and gain relevant experience.

en.title: Peace, Conflict and Violence: Core Concepts
en.short: Negative and positive peace, direct, structural and cultural violence, and how conflict differs from violence and war.

sections.heading: Peace: negative and positive
sections.text: Negative peace means the absence of direct violence, especially war. A ceasefire can bring negative peace while injustice and fear remain. Positive peace means the presence of conditions that make violence less likely: justice, cooperation, security and fair access to resources. Johan Galtung set out this distinction. Peace is therefore more than the silence of guns.

sections.heading: Conflict as incompatibility
sections.text: Conflict is a situation in which parties perceive their goals, interests or needs as incompatible. It can be latent or open, and it is not always harmful. A disagreement over land boundaries is conflict even if nobody is hurt. Conflict becomes violent only when parties use force or harm. War is a particular kind of organised, sustained armed conflict between political communities, often states. So conflict is broader than violence, and violence is broader than war.

sections.heading: Three forms of violence
sections.text: Direct violence is visible harm with an actor: killing, assault or forced displacement. Structural violence is harm built into institutions and social arrangements, such as unequal access to land, health care or schooling. It has no single attacker. Cultural violence is in beliefs, symbols and norms that justify the other two, for example a story that calls one group inferior. Galtung called these the violence triangle.

sections.heading: Case and distinctions
sections.text: Suppose two communities in northern Nigeria dispute a market site. The dispute is conflict. If youths burn stalls, that is direct violence. If permits always favour one group, that is structural violence. If leaders say the other group has no right to trade, that is cultural violence. None of this is automatically war; war requires organised armed fighting. The case shows why peace work must address all three forms.

keyPoints: Negative peace is the absence of direct violence; positive peace also includes justice and fair structures.
Conflict is a perceived incompatibility of goals or interests, not necessarily violence.
Direct violence is visible harm by an actor; structural violence is harm built into institutions; cultural violence justifies both.
War is organised armed conflict between political communities, so not every conflict or act of violence is war.
Galtung’s violence triangle links direct, structural and cultural violence.
Peace work must address all three forms of violence, not only stop fighting.

en.title: Levels and Types of Conflict
en.short: Intrapersonal to international levels, latent and manifest, violent and nonviolent, symmetric and asymmetric conflict.

sections.heading: Levels of conflict
sections.text: Conflict can be studied at several levels. Intrapersonal conflict is within one person, such as a student torn between study and paid work. Interpersonal conflict is between individuals. Group conflict is between teams, factions or identity groups. Organisational conflict occurs inside or between organisations over roles, resources or goals. Communal conflict is between communities or within a local community, often along identity lines. National conflict is within a state, involving government, regions or political movements. International conflict is between states or across borders. These levels are lenses, not boxes: a local water dispute can become national.

sections.heading: Latent and manifest
sections.text: A conflict is latent when the parties have incompatible interests or hostile feelings but do not act openly. It becomes manifest when they speak, organise, protest or fight. Latent conflict can be handled early; manifest conflict is visible and easier to analyse but harder to contain. Not all latent conflict becomes violent.

sections.heading: Violence and power
sections.text: Violent conflict uses physical force that injures people or damages property. Nonviolent conflict uses pressure such as strikes, boycotts, protests or legal action without physical violence. Symmetric conflict has parties of similar power and resources. Asymmetric conflict has a large power gap, for example a state against an armed group or an employer against workers. Asymmetry affects negotiation: the weaker side may need protection, allies or third-party support.

sections.heading: Illustrative case
sections.text: Suppose Amina’s and Musa’s neighbourhoods in a Nigerian town disagree over a new water pipe. At first people complain privately: latent. When one group blocks the road, it is manifest and nonviolent. If one neighbourhood has more money and council links, the conflict is asymmetric. If a state politician takes it up, it becomes national. The same dispute shows several levels and types at once.

keyPoints: Levels of conflict are analytical lenses; one conflict can operate at several levels.
Latent conflict is hidden incompatibility; manifest conflict is open action.
Violent conflict uses physical force; nonviolent conflict uses social, economic or political pressure.
Symmetric conflicts have similar power; asymmetric conflicts have a large power gap.
Communal conflict is between communities or within a local community, often along identity lines.
Naming the level and type helps choose the right response, such as early dialogue or protection for the weaker side.

en.title: Causes and Dynamics of Conflict
en.short: Root and proximate causes, grievances, interests, needs, identity, resources, power, escalation and the conflict cycle.

sections.heading: Root and proximate causes
sections.text: Root causes are the underlying conditions that make conflict likely: unequal access to land, exclusion from power, weak institutions, historical injustice or identity-based discrimination. Proximate causes are the nearer triggers that turn tension into open conflict, such as an election result, a killing, a price rise or a boundary dispute. Analysts separate the two because removing a trigger without addressing roots often leaves the conflict ready to restart.

sections.heading: Grievances, interests and needs
sections.text: A grievance is a belief that a group has been treated unfairly or denied something it is owed. Interests are what parties want: land, revenue, office, safety or recognition. Needs are deeper requirements for security, identity, participation and livelihood. Identity, such as ethnicity, religion, language or clan, can sharpen conflict when leaders mobilise it. Resources matter when they are scarce, valuable or captured by one group. Power is the ability to influence decisions, use force or control resources; unequal power turns disputes into domination.

sections.heading: Escalation and de-escalation
sections.text: Escalation is the move from disagreement to hostile acts: threats, protests, arrests, violence and wider alliances. De-escalation is the reverse: talks, concessions, mediation, exhaustion or third-party pressure. The conflict cycle describes how conflicts pass through latent tension, emergence, escalation, stalemate, de-escalation and settlement, then may return to latent tension. It is not a straight line; a settlement that ignores grievances can restart the cycle.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Consider a fictional case in Ghana. A mining company receives a licence on land that farmers in Nkura village use for crops. The root causes are unclear land title, youth unemployment and a history of the clan being ignored by district officials. The proximate trigger is a new fence across a footpath. Farmers Amina and Kojo organise a protest; arrests raise anger. Interests differ: the company wants profit, farmers want land and water, officials want revenue. Needs for food and recognition are unmet. Mediation, a boundary survey and compensation de-escalate the dispute.

keyPoints: Root causes are underlying conditions such as exclusion or weak institutions; proximate causes are the triggers that turn tension into open conflict.
A grievance is a perceived injustice, while an interest is what a party wants and a need is a deeper requirement for security or recognition.
Identity, resources and power shape how causes become conflict, especially when one group controls land, revenue or state authority.
Escalation moves from disagreement to hostile action, and de-escalation reverses it through talks, concessions or third-party pressure.
The conflict cycle is a loop, so a settlement that ignores root causes can allow conflict to return.

en.title: Theories of Conflict: Needs, Deprivation, Greed and Identity
en.short: Key theories of conflict and how they explain violent and nonviolent conflict.

sections.heading: Needs and deprivation
sections.text: Human needs theory, linked to John Burton, argues that conflict arises when basic needs such as security, recognition, identity and participation are unmet. These needs are not traded away easily, so suppressing them can make conflict persist. Relative deprivation is a different idea, associated with Ted Gurr. It is the gap between what people expect and what they believe they can get. The frustration can fuel protest or violence. Absolute poverty alone does not explain rebellion; perceived unfairness matters.

sections.heading: Greed, identity and structure
sections.text: Greed and grievance theory, associated with Paul Collier and Anke Hoeffler, asks whether armed groups fight for lootable resources or for political and social grievances. It stresses opportunity: resources can finance rebellion. Identity theories, drawing on social identity theory, show how group belonging and fear for a group’s future can sharpen conflict. Structural accounts focus on unequal institutions and horizontal inequalities, meaning inequalities between groups, as Frances Stewart describes. Consider a fictional town where a dam displaces farmers from one ethnic group while another group gains the contracts. Each theory could point to conflict, but each highlights a different cause.

sections.heading: Comparing explanations
sections.text: These theories are complements, not rivals. Needs and identity explain why people care deeply. Relative deprivation explains timing and mobilisation. Greed explains financing and persistence. Structural accounts explain who is excluded. Violent conflict is more likely when grievances are strong, identities are polarised, institutions are weak and armed groups can profit. Nonviolent conflict is more likely when people have peaceful channels, such as courts, elections, unions or protest, and when violence would cost them support. A theory that predicts violence should also ask why some deprived groups protest peacefully instead.

keyPoints: Human needs theory says unmet basic needs such as security, identity and participation drive conflict.
Relative deprivation is the perceived gap between expectations and attainable conditions, not poverty by itself.
Greed and grievance theory weighs economic opportunity and resources against political grievances.
Identity theories show how group belonging and fear for a group’s future can polarise conflict.
Structural accounts stress unequal institutions and horizontal inequalities between groups.
Violence is more likely when grievances, polarised identities, weak institutions and profit opportunities combine; peaceful channels make nonviolent conflict more likely.

en.title: Introduction to Conflict Analysis
en.short: Actors, issues, positions, interests and needs; timeline, conflict tree and ABC triangle for mapping a case.

sections.heading: Actors, issues and needs
sections.text:
Conflict analysis is the systematic study of a conflict before anyone acts on it. It asks who is involved, what the dispute is about and why it persists. Actors are people and groups who affect or are affected: primary parties with incompatible goals, secondary supporters, and third parties such as mediators.

Issues are the visible matters in dispute, such as land or representation. Below them lie positions, interests and needs. A position is what a party says it wants; an interest is the concern behind it; a need is a basic requirement a party believes it cannot surrender, such as safety, livelihood or recognition. Positions often clash; interests can sometimes be reconciled.

sections.heading: Timeline, tree and triangle
sections.text: Three tools organise it. A timeline lists events in date order, with turning points and past settlement attempts, so patterns and triggers become visible. A conflict tree draws the core problem as the trunk, root causes as roots and effects as branches; it stops analysts mistaking a symptom for a cause. The ABC triangle, associated with Johan Galtung, separates Attitude (perceptions, feelings, stereotypes), Behaviour (threats, violence, cooperation) and Contradiction (the incompatibility over issues). The sides interact: hostile attitudes harden behaviour, and violence deepens the contradiction.

sections.heading: Mapping a case
sections.text: Use the tools together. In an illustrative dispute over a borehole on contested land, a herders’ association demands that it stay open (position); dry-season water is its interest and livelihood its need. A farming cooperative demands that the fence come down (position); market access is its interest and recognition of ownership its need. A timeline shows the borehole built after an earlier boundary settlement, then a clash during a drought. The tree puts unclear land records at the root and school closure as an effect. The triangle records hostile attitudes, the clash as behaviour and the boundary as contradiction. Mapping points to clarifying records and sharing water, not only condemning the clash.

keyPoints: Conflict analysis identifies actors, issues and the reasons behind demands before action is taken.
A position is a stated demand; an interest is the concern behind it; a need is a basic requirement felt as non-negotiable.
A timeline orders events and reveals triggers, turning points and past attempts at settlement.
A conflict tree separates root causes (roots) from the core problem (trunk) and effects (branches).
The ABC triangle links Attitude, Behaviour and Contradiction, and each side can intensify the others.
Mapping a case with all three tools shows practical entry points, such as clarifying records or sharing a resource.

en.title: Histories of Peace Thought and Peace Movements
en.short: Religious and philosophical peace traditions, pacifism, internationalism, anti-war and civil rights movements.

sections.heading: Religious and philosophical roots
sections.text:
Religious traditions contain strong peace teachings. Christianity has the Sermon on the Mount and the command to love enemies; Islam greets with salaam (peace) and values reconciliation; Buddhism teaches non-harm (ahimsa) and compassion; Hinduism also teaches ahimsa. African traditional religions often stress community harmony and restorative settlement.

But most traditions also contain arguments for defensive war, so do not treat any religion as simply pacifist. Philosophical peace thought includes Stoic cosmopolitanism and Kant’s Perpetual Peace (1795), which proposed a federation of republics under law.

sections.heading: Pacifism and just war
sections.text:
Pacifism is the principled refusal of war or violence. Absolute pacifists reject all violence; conditional pacifists allow force only in extreme cases. Historic peace churches such as the Quakers (Society of Friends), Mennonites and Church of the Brethren are known for pacifism.

The just war tradition, shaped by Augustine and Thomas Aquinas, is not pacifist: it asks when war can be justified and how it must be limited. Both traditions matter because they debate the moral limits of force.

sections.heading: Internationalism and anti-war movements
sections.text:
Internationalism is the belief that states should cooperate through law and institutions. After the First World War, the League of Nations and peace societies tried to settle disputes without war; after the Second World War, the United Nations was founded.

Anti-war movements, including women’s peace campaigns and nuclear disarmament campaigns, pressed governments to limit arms. These movements gave the field its concern with law, disarmament and public mobilisation.

sections.heading: Civil rights and peace
sections.text:
Civil rights movements linked peace with justice. Gandhi’s campaigns in India and Martin Luther King Jr.'s in the United States argued that oppression is a form of violence. The anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa combined nonviolent protest with armed resistance after 1961.

In Liberia, Leymah Gbowee led the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace from 2002, using prayer and sit-ins to press for an end to the civil war, which ended in 2003. Such movements shaped peace studies by showing that peace requires equality and that ordinary people can act. They also gave the field its case studies and moral vocabulary.

keyPoints: Religious traditions contain peace teachings but also arguments for defensive war; they are not simply pacifist.
Pacifism rejects war or violence, absolutely or conditionally, while just war theory asks when force can be justified and limited.
Internationalism seeks peace through law and institutions such as the League of Nations and the United Nations.
Anti-war movements pressed for disarmament and public mobilisation.
Civil rights movements linked peace with justice and showed that oppression is a form of violence.
The Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace, begun in 2002, is an African example of a peace movement led by Leymah Gbowee.

en.title: Human Rights, Justice and Peace
en.short: UDHR, rights frameworks, distributive and restorative justice, and how grievances feed conflict or peace.
keywords: African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights

sections.heading: Rights frameworks
sections.text: Human rights are entitlements that every person has simply because they are human. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1948, sets out civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights. Its first article says: “All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.” The UDHR is a declaration, not a treaty. Two binding treaties, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), were adopted in 1966 and came into force in 1976. Other treaties include the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC, 1989) and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW, 1979). Regional systems include the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (1981). States have duties to respect, protect and fulfil rights.

sections.heading: Two kinds of justice
sections.text: Justice asks how goods, opportunities and harms should be shared and repaired. Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of resources and burdens. John Rawls argued that inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged. Restorative justice concerns harm. Instead of asking only how to punish an offender, it asks how to repair the victim, the community and the relationship, through acknowledgement, apology, restitution and dialogue. It is not the same as retribution, which focuses on punishment.

sections.heading: Case and conflict link
sections.text: Rights claims and justice grievances can drive conflict. When groups believe their land, language, religion or access to services is denied, they may mobilise. Yet rights claims can also build peace if institutions hear them fairly. Consider a fictional town, Bwala, where a mining licence displaces farmers. Residents claim rights to property, water and consultation; the company holds a permit. Distributive justice would ask how benefits and compensation are shared. Restorative justice would ask the company to acknowledge harm, restore land where possible and meet the community. A negotiated settlement, not violence, can turn grievance into reform. Peace therefore needs courts, mediation and political inclusion that can settle claims without denying dignity.

keyPoints: The UDHR was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948 and is a declaration, not a treaty.
The ICCPR and ICESCR are binding UN treaties adopted in 1966 and in force from 1976.
States have duties to respect, protect and fulfil human rights.
Distributive justice concerns fair sharing of resources and burdens; restorative justice concerns repairing harm through acknowledgement and dialogue.
Rights claims and justice grievances can mobilise conflict, but fair institutions can turn them into peaceful reform.
Peace work links rights protection, fair distribution and repair of harm.

en.title: Evidence and Inquiry in Peace and Conflict Studies
en.short: Sources, argument, bias, case comparison, qualitative and quantitative evidence, and research ethics.

sections.heading: Sources and claims
sections.text: Evidence is information used to support a claim. A primary source is first-hand material, such as an interview, a treaty text, a court record or an observer’s field notes. A secondary source analyses primary material, such as a journal article or a textbook. Official sources, reports by non-governmental organisations (NGOs), news reports and testimony have strengths and limits. Ask who produced a source, for what purpose, and what it leaves out.

sections.heading: Argument and bias
sections.text: An argument is a claim supported by reasons and evidence. Separate the claim from the evidence and from the inference that links them. Bias is a systematic slant that pushes evidence in one direction. It can come from the researcher, the source or the method. Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice evidence that fits a preferred view. Triangulation means checking a finding against independent sources, methods or people. It reduces bias but does not remove it.

sections.heading: Comparing cases
sections.text: Case comparison studies several cases using the same criteria. Choose cases for a reason, state what is similar and what differs, and avoid choosing cases that prove your point. Qualitative evidence, such as interviews, focus groups, documents and observation, helps explain meaning and process. Quantitative evidence, such as counts, rates, surveys and datasets, helps measure patterns. A correlation is a relationship between two variables, things that can be measured; it does not prove causation.

sections.heading: Ethics and example
sections.text: Ethical use of evidence means informed consent (people freely agree after learning the study), confidentiality, do no harm, data security and accurate citation. Do not invent, alter or quote out of context. Protect vulnerable people and get permission before recording. Example: a student compares two communities in Kaduna State, Nigeria, one with a peace committee and one without. She interviews residents and officials, reads minutes and counts incidents from police and NGO logs. Fewer incidents are reported in the committee town. She cannot conclude the committee caused this, as reporting may differ. She reports limits and protects identities.

keyPoints: A claim is not evidence; an argument links a claim to reasons and evidence.
Primary sources are first-hand; secondary sources analyse them.
Triangulation checks a finding against independent sources, methods or people.
Qualitative evidence explains meaning and process; quantitative evidence measures patterns.
Correlation does not prove causation.
Ethical use of evidence requires informed consent, confidentiality, do no harm and accurate citation.

en.title: Conflict Prevention and Early Warning
en.short: Structural and operational prevention, early warning indicators, preventive diplomacy and the warning-response gap.

sections.heading: Two kinds of prevention
sections.text: Prevention is usually split into structural and operational. Structural prevention addresses root causes over years: exclusion, inequality, weak rule of law, disputed land and youth unemployment. Operational prevention acts when violence is imminent: crisis diplomacy, mediation, confidence-building, monitoring and targeted pressure. The split is analytical. Effective policy links long-term reform to immediate measures, because root causes do not wait quietly while a crisis is managed.

sections.heading: Indicators and early warning
sections.text: An indicator is an observable condition that raises or lowers the risk of violence, such as rising hate speech, armed group recruitment, disputed elections, food price spikes or displacement. An early warning system collects such data, analyses patterns and issues risk assessments with response options. It is probabilistic, not prophecy: false alarms and missed warnings both happen. Good systems combine local reporting with national and regional analysis, and they state clearly what would count as evidence of worsening risk.

sections.heading: Preventive diplomacy
sections.text: Preventive diplomacy is diplomatic action to stop disputes arising, escalating or spreading. The 1992 UN report An Agenda for Peace used this definition. Warning often fails to produce response. The warning-response gap comes from weak political will, sovereignty concerns, competing crises, poor coordination and unclear responsibility. A warning system needs a linked response mechanism: named decision-makers, budgets, timelines and accountability. Without that link, a good report can become a record of what was known before failure.

sections.heading: Illustrative case
sections.text: Imagine a fictional district, Kolo, before an election. An early warning team reports rising land disputes, militia recruitment and hate speech. Structural prevention would fund land registration and youth employment. Operational prevention would send mediators and monitor rallies. If the report sits unread because no agency owns the response, the gap between warning and response has caused the harm.

keyPoints: Structural prevention addresses root causes over years, while operational prevention responds to imminent violence.
An indicator is an observable condition that changes the assessed risk of conflict.
Early warning systems collect and analyse indicators and issue response options; they are probabilistic, not prophecy.
Preventive diplomacy aims to stop disputes arising, escalating or spreading.
The warning-response gap is the failure to act on credible warnings, often because of weak political will, sovereignty concerns and poor coordination.
Effective early warning needs a named response mechanism with budgets, timelines and accountability.

en.title: Negotiation: Theory and Practice
en.short: Distributive and integrative bargaining, BATNA, interests, stages, culture and ethics in negotiation.

sections.heading: Two bargaining styles
sections.text: Negotiation is discussion between parties who want different outcomes but need agreement. In distributive bargaining they divide a fixed amount, such as a price or salary. One side’s gain is the other’s loss, so the style is competitive: claim value. Integrative bargaining seeks to create value. Parties trade issues they value differently, called logrolling, so both can gain. Most real negotiations mix both styles.

sections.heading: BATNA and interests
sections.text: Before bargaining, know your BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. A strong BATNA gives leverage because you can walk away. The zone of possible agreement (ZOPA) is the range between the parties’ walk-away points; no deal is possible if they do not overlap. Skilled negotiators separate positions from interests. A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why. Interests often allow more options.

sections.heading: Stages of negotiation
sections.text: Negotiation usually passes through preparation, opening, exploration, bargaining and closing. Preparation covers facts, interests, BATNA and options. Opening sets tone and agenda. Exploration shares information and tests assumptions. Bargaining exchanges proposals and concessions. Closing records the agreement; implementation follows. Case: Ngozi wants a shop lease. Her position is 40,000 naira a month; her interest is a three-year term near a market. The landlord’s position is 60,000; his interest is a reliable tenant. They agree on 50,000 for three years with a repair clause, creating value through terms, not only price.

sections.heading: Culture and ethics
sections.text: Culture shapes negotiation. Edward Hall distinguished high-context cultures, where meaning rests on relationships and indirect cues, from low-context cultures, where people speak directly. Individualist and collectivist norms affect who speaks and how decisions are made. These are tendencies, not rules about individuals. Ethics asks what conduct is fair: honesty about facts, avoiding coercion and improper inducements, and keeping confidences. A negotiator may conceal a walk-away price, but lying about a material fact can destroy trust and the deal.

keyPoints: Distributive bargaining claims value from a fixed amount; integrative bargaining creates value by trading issues.
BATNA is the best alternative to a negotiated agreement and sets your walk-away point.
ZOPA is the overlap between the parties’ walk-away points; no overlap means no deal.
Positions are stated demands, while interests are underlying needs that allow more options.
The stages are preparation, opening, exploration, bargaining and closing.
Culture shapes style but does not predict individuals, and ethics requires honesty, no coercion and confidentiality.

en.title: Mediation, Arbitration and Adjudication: The Third-Party Spectrum
en.short: Third-party roles from facilitation and mediation to arbitration and adjudication, with consent and ethics.

sections.heading: The third-party spectrum
sections.text: Third-party dispute resolution runs from facilitation to adjudication. A facilitator helps people communicate and set an agenda but does not propose terms. A mediator is neutral and helps the parties reach their own agreement; the mediator controls process, not outcome. An arbitrator hears the parties and decides the dispute, and the award is binding. Adjudication means a court or statutory tribunal decides according to law. Along the spectrum the third party gains control over the outcome and the parties lose it.

sections.heading: Process and consent
sections.text: Consent and process differ. Mediation is voluntary: parties can leave, and any settlement must be theirs. A typical process has opening statements, joint sessions, private caucuses and a written agreement. Arbitration also rests on consent, usually an arbitration clause. The parties appoint arbitrators, exchange pleadings, attend a hearing and receive an award. Adjudication needs no defendant consent; state courts have compulsory jurisdiction. All three roles demand impartiality: mediators and arbitrators should disclose conflicts, and judges must recuse themselves when conflicted.

sections.heading: Enforceability and ethics
sections.text: Enforceability differs. A mediated settlement is a contract; if broken, the other side can sue on it, subject to national law. An arbitration award is binding and, in international commercial cases, widely enforceable under the New York Convention 1958, with limited grounds to refuse. Domestic arbitration statutes vary, so check current law. A court judgment is enforced through the court’s machinery. Ethics require confidentiality where promised, informed consent, competence and care about power imbalances. A mediator must not pressure parties.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Consider Amina and Tunde, who dispute a shop lease in Kano, Nigeria. A facilitator helps them clarify rent and repair terms. A mediator then helps them agree a rent reduction and repair schedule. If mediation fails and their contract has an arbitration clause, an arbitrator decides. If not, Amina may sue in court. The case shows how consent, impartiality and enforceability shift along the spectrum.

keyPoints: Facilitation helps communication; mediation helps parties reach their own agreement; arbitration and adjudication decide the dispute.
Mediation and arbitration rest on consent, while adjudication uses the compulsory jurisdiction of courts.
Impartiality requires mediators and arbitrators to disclose conflicts and judges to recuse themselves when conflicted.
A mediated settlement is a contract; an arbitration award is binding and widely enforceable under the New York Convention 1958 in contracting states; a court judgment is enforced by the court.
Ethics in third-party roles include informed consent, confidentiality, competence and attention to power imbalances.
The further along the spectrum, the more control the third party has over the outcome.

en.title: Dialogue, Reconciliation and Apology
en.short: Intergroup dialogue, truth-telling, apology, forgiveness and the difference between reconciliation and coexistence.

sections.heading: Dialogue and truth-telling
sections.text: Intergroup dialogue is a facilitated, structured conversation between people from groups with different experiences, often unequal power. It aims at mutual understanding, not bargaining or winning. Truth-telling means naming harms publicly and listening to those affected. It can happen in commissions, community meetings or oral history projects. Truth alone does not repair relationships, but without acknowledgement, trust is hard to rebuild.

sections.heading: Apology and forgiveness
sections.text: An apology is a statement that admits a wrong, accepts responsibility, expresses regret and commits to change. A credible public apology usually names the harm, the victims and the duty to prevent repetition; reparations, meaning compensation or other redress for victims, may accompany it. Forgiveness is the harmed person’s voluntary decision to release resentment. It cannot be demanded, and it is not the same as legal pardon or amnesty. Apology may invite forgiveness, but reconciliation does not depend on every victim forgiving.

sections.heading: Reconciliation versus coexistence
sections.text: Reconciliation is a contested term. Thin reconciliation means groups stop fighting and accept each other’s right to exist. Thick reconciliation adds trust, mutual recognition and a shared future. Coexistence is living together without violence, but it may still involve segregation or inequality. A settlement is an agreement that ends a dispute, often through compensation or a boundary, without repairing relationships. Reconciliation therefore goes beyond both coexistence and settlement.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Consider a fictional town where farmers and herders clash over land. A ceasefire and compensation settle the immediate dispute. Coexistence begins when violence stops. Reconciliation grows through facilitated dialogue, public testimony about losses, a community apology, rebuilding a shared market and a joint monitoring committee. The test is not only whether the deal holds, but whether the groups can work together and trust the process.

keyPoints: Dialogue aims at mutual understanding, not negotiation or debate.
Truth-telling publicly acknowledges harms and gives victims a hearing.
A credible apology admits responsibility, expresses regret and commits to non-repetition.
Forgiveness is voluntary and cannot be required by apology or settlement.
Coexistence means living without violence; reconciliation adds trust and mutual recognition.
A settlement ends a dispute but may not repair relationships.

en.title: Nonviolence and Civil Resistance
en.short: Theories of nonviolent power, tactics, campaigns, state responses, and limits.

sections.heading: Power and consent
sections.text:
Nonviolence is the deliberate refusal to use physical force, often combined with active protest. Civil resistance is collective, organised action by ordinary people, such as strikes, boycotts and sit-ins, to challenge injustice without violence. A central theory, associated with Gene Sharp, holds that rulers depend on the cooperation and obedience of many people. If that cooperation is withdrawn, their power weakens.

Nonviolent action can work through conversion, when opponents change their beliefs; accommodation, when they concede; or coercion, when the system is paralysed. Critics stress that power is also shaped by institutions, resources and divisions inside the state, so consent is not the whole story.

sections.heading: Tactics and campaigns
sections.text:
Sharp grouped methods into protest and persuasion, noncooperation (refusing to assist authorities), and intervention (direct action such as blockades). Campaigns combine methods over time and link demands to wider audiences.

In the Indian Salt March of 1930, Gandhi and followers walked about 240 miles over 24 days to Dandi to make salt in defiance of the British salt tax. The march was symbolic protest, civil disobedience (openly breaking an unjust law) and mass mobilisation. It did not end colonial rule at once, but it exposed the law’s injustice and widened the independence movement. Campaigns need clear aims, discipline, training and plans for repression.

sections.heading: State responses and limits
sections.text:
States may respond with arrests, bans, surveillance, force, co-optation (buying off leaders), or partial concessions. Repression can backfire when it creates sympathy and splits the regime, but it can also crush a movement.

Nonviolent action carries risks: participants may be injured or killed, movements may fragment, and violence by infiltrators or police can destroy discipline. It is not automatically successful. It tends to be weaker where the regime is willing to kill on a large scale, where opposition is fragmented, or where demands are unclear. Success depends on broad participation, organisation, allies and strategy, not only moral appeal.

keyPoints: Nonviolence is active and deliberate, not passive acceptance.
Civil resistance uses organised methods such as strikes, boycotts and civil disobedience.
Consent theory says rulers depend on cooperation, so withdrawal of consent can weaken them.
Sharp grouped methods as protest and persuasion, noncooperation, and intervention.
Repression can backfire but can also crush movements, so risks must be planned for.
Success depends on participation, organisation, allies and strategy, not moral appeal alone.

en.title: Peacemaking, Peacekeeping and Ceasefire Monitoring
en.short: Distinguishes peacemaking, peacekeeping and ceasefire monitoring, and explains UN principles and mandate limits.

sections.heading: Three related roles
sections.text: Peacemaking is diplomatic action to bring parties to a settlement. It includes mediation, negotiation and good offices, where a third party offers a channel for talks, and may be led by the United Nations (UN), a regional body or a respected state. Peacekeeping is the deployment of military, police and civilian personnel under an international mandate to support a ceasefire or peace agreement. Ceasefire monitoring is the technical work of observing, verifying and reporting compliance with a ceasefire. Monitors liaise with commanders, record violations and build confidence. Monitoring may sit inside a peacekeeping mission or be run separately. Peace enforcement is different: it uses force under Chapter VII without full consent.

sections.heading: UN peacekeeping principles
sections.text: UN peacekeeping rests on three principles. Consent means the main parties accept the mission. Impartiality means the mission implements its mandate without favouring a side; it is not neutrality, because monitors must report violations. Minimum use of force means force is used only as a last resort, traditionally in self-defence and now often to defend the mandate or protect civilians. The principles support one another. If consent collapses, a mission may become a party to the conflict.

sections.heading: Mandates and limits
sections.text:
UN mission mandates come from the Security Council. Chapter VI missions are consent-based; Chapter VII missions may authorise enforcement. Limits are real: mandates may be broad while troops, transport and access are scarce. Host states may restrict movement, and troop contributors may set caveats, meaning limits on how their soldiers can be used. Monitors are usually unarmed and cannot stop violations; they can only report and refer them to political channels.

Illustration: in the fictional state of Bantura, a ceasefire creates a 10 km buffer. Monitors log 12 violations in one week: 7 shooting incidents, 3 patrols into the buffer and 2 supply convoys. They cannot halt them. They report to a Joint Monitoring Committee, which asks commanders Amina and Kwame to meet. Peacemakers then negotiate a patrol timetable, and monitors verify it.

keyPoints: Peacemaking seeks a settlement; peacekeeping supports implementation; ceasefire monitoring verifies compliance.
UN peacekeeping principles are consent, impartiality and minimum use of force.
Impartiality is not neutrality: missions must report violations without favouring a side.
UN mandates come from the Security Council; Chapter VI relies on consent, while Chapter VII can authorise enforcement.
Monitors are usually unarmed and cannot enforce a ceasefire; their reports feed political and diplomatic action.
Broad mandates do not remove limits of troops, access, host-state consent and contributor caveats.

en.title: Peacebuilding and Post-Conflict Reconstruction
en.short: Liberal peacebuilding, local ownership, institutions, livelihoods, security sector reform, reconciliation and critiques.

sections.heading: Liberal peacebuilding
sections.text: Liberal peacebuilding is external and local support for rebuilding a state after war around three ideas: market democracy, the rule of law and professional security forces. It assumes that elections, civil society and open markets make renewed war less likely. The model became common in the 1990s and 2000s, often through United Nations missions. Roland Paris warned that rapid political and market liberalisation can destabilise a fragile state, so institutions should be built before competition is opened.

sections.heading: Ownership and institutions
sections.text: Local ownership means the host society sets priorities and leads reconstruction, with outsiders advising and funding. It is more than consultation. If donors write the strategy and local groups only sign it, ownership is token. Institutions matter: courts, parliaments, audit offices, tax systems and election bodies must be legitimate and able to work. A fictional example: in Bantala, a town recovering from civil war, a women’s market association drafts the livelihood plan, while a UN agency funds it and the district council audits spending. This is ownership with accountability.

sections.heading: Livelihoods and security
sections.text: Livelihoods are the ways people earn and feed themselves: jobs, land access, markets, credit and basic services. Reconstruction that builds ministries but ignores them can leave ex-combatants and displaced families without income. Security sector reform (SSR) means reshaping the army, police, courts and prisons so they protect civilians and answer to civilian oversight. Training alone is not enough; pay, discipline, vetting and laws must change.

sections.heading: Reconciliation and critique
sections.text: Reconciliation is the rebuilding of trust between groups after violence, through dialogue, truth telling, apology and shared projects. It cannot be decreed from outside. Critics say external-led reconstruction is too top-down and template-driven. It can weaken local agency, import unsuitable market reforms and create shallow institutions that collapse when donors leave. Supporters answer that outside resources and monitoring are needed where local capacity and trust are low. The practical task is to combine external support with real local control.

keyPoints: Liberal peacebuilding links peace to market democracy, the rule of law and professional security forces.
Local ownership means host actors lead priorities and decisions, not just consent to donor plans.
Legitimate institutions, not only elections, are needed for lasting reconstruction.
Livelihoods and security sector reform address daily safety and income, which shape whether peace holds.
Reconciliation requires dialogue, truth telling and shared action; it cannot be imposed from outside.
Critics call external-led reconstruction top-down and template-driven; supporters stress resources and monitoring where local capacity is weak.

en.title: Transitional Justice
en.short: Trials, truth commissions, reparations, amnesty and vetting, memory and victims, and the peace versus justice debate.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Transitional justice is the set of measures a society uses to address large-scale human rights abuses after war or authoritarian rule. Its aims include acknowledging victims, establishing facts, holding wrongdoers to account and reforming institutions. Common tools are criminal trials, truth commissions, reparations, amnesty and vetting. No single tool does everything; societies combine them in different ways.

sections.heading: Trials and truths
sections.text: Criminal trials, domestic or international, establish individual guilt and may deter future abuse. Examples include the Nuremberg trials after the Second World War and the International Criminal Court, which began work in 2002 under the Rome Statute. Trials are slow and costly. Truth commissions are official bodies that record patterns of abuse and hear victims. South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, set up in the 1990s, heard testimony and could grant amnesty to people who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes. Amnesty is a legal exemption from prosecution. Vetting screens officials for past abuses and removes those unfit to serve.

sections.heading: Reparations and memory
sections.text: Reparations are benefits given to victims to repair harm. They may be material, such as money or health care, or symbolic, such as apologies and memorials. Memory work includes archives, museums and public commemorations that keep past abuses visible. A victim-centred approach asks survivors what they need and treats them as participants, not only witnesses. Reparations and memory can support dignity and social trust, but they can also be uneven or politically controlled.

sections.heading: Peace versus justice
sections.text: The central debate is whether to prosecute wrongdoers or to grant amnesty for the sake of peace. Prosecutions may destabilise a fragile peace and make armed leaders refuse to disarm. Amnesty may end fighting but leave victims without justice and weaken the rule of law. Some argue for sequencing: secure peace first, then pursue justice. Others reply that impunity undermines lasting peace. There is no universal answer; the choice depends on context, and hybrid approaches are common.

keyPoints: Transitional justice addresses past abuses through trials, truth commissions, reparations, amnesty and vetting.
Trials establish individual guilt; truth commissions record patterns of abuse and hear victims.
Amnesty is a legal exemption from prosecution; conditional amnesty usually requires full disclosure.
Vetting removes officials linked to past abuses from public service.
Reparations may be material or symbolic, and memory work keeps past abuses visible.
The peace versus justice debate asks whether prosecutions or amnesty better support lasting peace; context matters.

en.title: Gender, Conflict and Peace
en.short: Masculinities, femininities, gender-based violence, women’s participation, UNSCR 1325 and gendered peacebuilding.

sections.heading: Gender as power
sections.text: Gender is the social meaning given to being male or female, not sex itself. Masculinities are ideals and practices of manhood; femininities are ideals and practices of womanhood. Both are plural and change over time. Raewyn Connell’s hegemonic masculinity is the culturally dominant form that helps justify men’s power over women and other men. Not all men are violent and not all women are peaceful, but gender norms shape who fights, who is protected and who speaks.

sections.heading: Violence and protection
sections.text: Sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) is violence directed at people because of gender or affecting them differently by gender. It includes rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, trafficking, intimate partner violence and harassment. In war it is sometimes used as a weapon against civilians. Men and boys are also victims, though shame and fear often stop reporting. Protection means health care, psychosocial support, legal aid and justice, not only guards at camps.

sections.heading: Women’s participation and 1325
sections.text: Women are often excluded from formal peace talks, yet they do much informal peace work. UN Security Council Resolution 1325, adopted in 2000, calls for women’s equal participation in conflict prevention, negotiations, peacekeeping and reconstruction. It also calls for protection from conflict-related sexual violence. Many states have National Action Plans to implement it, but practice varies. In Liberia, the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace, led by Leymah Gbowee, used strikes and sit-ins to press for peace and women’s voice in the 2003 process.

sections.heading: Gendered peacebuilding
sections.text: Gendered peacebuilding means designing post-war recovery so that it tackles gender inequalities. It includes gender mainstreaming, which checks how policies affect women, men, girls and boys. Practical steps include women’s seats in decision-making, safe reparations, SGBV services, and support for women’s groups. It also means working with men and boys on nonviolent forms of masculinity. Without this, peace may last for some but leave others unsafe.

keyPoints: Gender is a social construction, not the same as sex, and masculinities and femininities are plural and shape power.
Sexual and gender-based violence includes rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, trafficking and intimate partner violence, and men and boys can also be victims.
Women are often excluded from formal peace talks even though they do much informal peace work.
UN Security Council Resolution 1325, adopted in 2000, calls for women’s equal participation and for protection from conflict-related sexual violence.
National Action Plans are the common way states implement Resolution 1325, but practice varies by country.
Gendered peacebuilding uses gender mainstreaming and addresses inequalities, reparations, SGBV services and nonviolent forms of masculinity.

en.title: Religion, Ethnicity and Conflict
en.short: Identity and mobilisation, religious and ethnic framing, religious peacemaking, and avoiding essentialism.

sections.heading: Identity and mobilisation
sections.text:
Ethnicity is a sense of belonging based on shared descent, language or culture; religion is a system of belief and practice that also shapes community. Neither is fixed. Most scholars today take a constructivist view: boundaries between groups are made and remade through history, intermarriage, migration and politics.

Diversity alone rarely causes violence. Conflict needs mobilisation, the process by which leaders turn a category into a political actor. Ethnic or religious entrepreneurs name grievances, promise security and organise followers. Where the state is weak or exclusionary, this is easier.

sections.heading: Framing conflict
sections.text:
Framing is the way a conflict is described, and the description shapes the response. Calling a struggle a religious war may attract outside support and silence compromise; calling it a land dispute may open negotiation. Framing often works by metonymy: one incident, such as a riot or a blasphemy case, is presented as the whole relationship between two groups.

Elites do manipulate frames, but a frame succeeds only when it resonates with real experience of injustice. So framing is not simply invented.

sections.heading: Religious peacemaking
sections.text: Religious actors do peacemaking in several ways: interfaith councils that calm rumours, clergy who mediate, and transnational communities that host talks. In Mozambique, the Community of Sant’Egidio, a Catholic lay community based in Rome, helped mediate between Frelimo and Renamo, leading to the 1992 Rome General Peace Accords. Religious leaders can also legitimise war, so their peacemaking role is not automatic.

sections.heading: Avoiding essentialism
sections.text: Essentialism is the error of treating a group as having a fixed, uniform character: 'the X are violent'. It ignores internal disagreement, change over time and mixed motives. Better analysis asks who is mobilising, which grievances are real, which institutions have failed, and which leaders gain. Essentialist explanations also make peace harder, because they suggest the problem is the people rather than the politics.

keyPoints: Ethnic and religious identities are socially constructed and change over time.
Diversity alone does not cause conflict; mobilisation by leaders turns categories into political actors.
Framing a conflict as religious or ethnic shapes who supports it and whether compromise is possible.
Frames succeed only when they connect with real grievances, so they are not pure invention.
Religious actors can make peace, as in Mozambique in 1992, but can also legitimise war.
Essentialism treats groups as uniform and fixed, and it obstructs peace.

en.title: Natural Resources, Environment and Conflict
en.short: Greed and scarcity, land, oil and minerals, climate stress, conflict resources and environmental peacebuilding.

sections.heading: Greed and scarcity
sections.text: Two broad explanations link resources to conflict. Scarcity means demand for land, water or grazing exceeds supply, so groups compete. Abundance means valuable resources such as oil or diamonds can be captured and sold, financing armed groups. This is the greed argument. Neither is automatic. The resource curse is the tendency for mineral wealth to accompany weak institutions, corruption and conflict. Whether it happens depends on institutions, revenue sharing and who controls the resource.

sections.heading: Land, oil and minerals
sections.text: Land conflict often grows from unclear tenure, dispossession and unequal access. When farmers and herders compete for shrinking pasture and water, disputes can turn violent. Oil and minerals bring revenue but also pollution, enclave economies and struggles over shares. An enclave economy is one where the resource sector creates few local jobs and few links to the wider economy. A conflict resource is a natural resource whose extraction or trade helps fund armed conflict. Diamonds, gold and coltan, a mineral used in electronics, have all been linked to fighting. The Kimberley Process certifies rough diamonds, yet weak monitoring and smuggling limit it.

sections.heading: Climate stress
sections.text: Climate change acts as a risk multiplier. Drought, floods and sea-level rise can destroy livelihoods, displace people and sharpen competition over water and grazing. They rarely cause conflict alone. Conflict depends on governance, inequality and existing grievances. Climate adaptation, early warning and fair water sharing can reduce risk. Badly planned projects, such as dams or large land deals, can also create new disputes.

sections.heading: Environmental peacebuilding
sections.text: Environmental peacebuilding uses environmental cooperation and natural resource management to build peace. Examples include joint river commissions, peace parks, which are protected areas shared across borders, and programmes that restore land and livelihoods. It works best when communities share benefits and when agreements are transparent. In the Niger Delta, oil pollution and unfair revenue sharing have fed grievances. Clean-up, compensation and transparent revenue allocation can support peace, but they cannot replace political reform.

keyPoints: Resource scarcity and resource abundance can both contribute to conflict, but neither does so automatically.
A conflict resource is a resource whose extraction or trade funds armed groups.
The resource curse is the tendency for mineral wealth to accompany weak institutions and conflict.
Climate change is best understood as a risk multiplier rather than a sole cause of conflict.
Environmental peacebuilding uses shared environmental management to build trust and reduce conflict.
Land tenure, revenue sharing and transparency are central to preventing resource conflicts.

en.title: Development, Security and Humanitarian Action
en.short: The aid, development and security nexus, humanitarian principles, do no harm and aid in conflict.

sections.heading: The triple nexus
sections.text: Development, security and humanitarian action are distinct fields. Development works over years to reduce poverty and build institutions. Security aims to protect people and states from violence. Humanitarian action saves lives in emergencies and is guided by need alone. The triple nexus is the policy idea that humanitarian, development and peace actors should coordinate in protracted crises. Critics warn that merging them can make aid serve political or military aims.

sections.heading: Humanitarian principles
sections.text: Humanitarian principles are core standards. Humanity means human suffering must be addressed wherever it is found. Impartiality means aid is given by need alone, without discrimination. Neutrality means humanitarians do not take sides in hostilities or political disputes. Independence means aid is not controlled by political, military or economic actors. These principles help agencies gain access and trust. They are ideals, and in war they are often hard to apply.

sections.heading: Do no harm
sections.text: Do no harm is a framework for checking whether aid helps or worsens conflict. Mary B. Anderson set it out in the 1990s. Aid brings resources such as food, jobs and contracts. These can feed war economies or strengthen one group. Aid also sends messages about who is helped, hired or protected. A do no harm analysis maps dividers that separate groups and connectors that link them. In a fictional case, an agency in Riverland hires a local militia to guard food convoys. The militia is a party to the conflict, so the agency may be seen as taking sides.

sections.heading: Securitisation and aid
sections.text: Securitisation is the process by which an issue is framed as an existential threat requiring emergency measures beyond normal politics. The term comes from the Copenhagen School, especially Ole Wæver and Barry Buzan. When aid is securitised, it is tied to military or counterinsurgency goals. This can blur humanitarian space, the room for neutral and impartial agencies to operate, and expose aid workers to attack. Coordination with security actors may be needed for access, but agencies must weigh the risks.

keyPoints: Development, security and humanitarian action have different aims but overlap in protracted crises.
The four humanitarian principles are humanity, impartiality, neutrality and independence.
Do no harm asks whether aid resources and messages strengthen dividers or connectors in conflict.
Securitisation frames an issue as an existential threat requiring emergency measures.
Securitised aid can blur humanitarian space and expose aid workers to attack.
Coordination with security actors may help access but must be weighed against humanitarian principles.

en.title: Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration
en.short: Phases, combatant needs, weapons management, security sector reform links and risks of DDR.

sections.heading: Three phases
sections.text: Disarmament is the collection, documentation, control and disposal of weapons, ammunition and explosives held by combatants and armed groups. Demobilisation is the formal and controlled discharge of active combatants from armed forces or groups. It usually includes cantonment, registration, screening, identity papers, transport, food, health checks and a reinsertion allowance. Reintegration is the longer process by which ex-combatants gain civilian status, livelihoods and acceptance in communities. It has economic, social and political parts. The three phases overlap; DDR is not a single event.

sections.heading: Combatant needs
sections.text: Combatants need safety, food, shelter, health care, trauma support, family contact and clear information about benefits. Women, children and persons with disabilities need separate, protected arrangements. Children associated with armed forces or groups should be released and reintegrated through child protection services, not treated as adult fighters. Programmes work better when combatants are consulted and when receiving communities also get support, so that reintegration does not look like a reward for violence.

sections.heading: Weapons and SSR
sections.text: Weapons management covers stockpile security, marking and tracing, destruction, and control of small arms. Buy-back schemes can help but may create markets for new weapons. DDR should link to security sector reform (SSR): reform of the army, police, courts and oversight bodies. DDR reduces and disarms fighters; SSR builds legitimate, accountable security institutions. One cannot replace the other. National ownership and a clear legal framework matter.

sections.heading: Risks and example
sections.text: Risks include spoilers, re-recruitment, diverted weapons, corruption, exclusion, stigma and community resentment. DDR can fail if ceasefire and security guarantees are weak. Example: in a fictional district, Kpana, a peace agreement provides for 300 fighters to enter cantonment. Registration finds 40 are children, who are released to child protection. Adults receive allowances and training. The programme also funds a market for the host town. This reduces resentment and makes return safer. The numbers are illustrative only.

keyPoints: Disarmament collects and controls weapons; demobilisation discharges combatants; reintegration restores civilian life.
DDR must address safety, health, trauma, family and livelihood needs, with special protection for women and children.
Weapons management includes stockpile security, marking, tracing and destruction.
DDR supports but cannot replace security sector reform.
Weak security guarantees, spoilers, corruption and exclusion can cause DDR to fail.
Support for receiving communities reduces resentment and improves reintegration.

en.title: Research Methods in Peace and Conflict Studies
en.short: Qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods, design, fieldwork, ethics, safety, conflict sensitivity and data quality.

sections.heading: Design and methods
sections.text: Research design is the plan that links a question to evidence. A qualitative study asks how people interpret conflict, using interviews, focus groups or documents, and analyses words and meanings. A quantitative study measures variables and tests relationships with surveys or statistics. Mixed methods combine both, using one to explain or check the other. Sampling is choosing who or what to study; explain how you chose cases or respondents, because this limits what you can claim. Triangulation means checking a finding against a second source, method or researcher. A good design also states the limits of the evidence.

sections.heading: Fieldwork, ethics and safety
sections.text: Fieldwork in conflict settings needs permission, local partners and a clear plan for access. Informed consent means telling participants the purpose, risks and their right to stop. Confidentiality protects identities; anonymise notes and store data securely. Do no harm and conflict sensitivity mean asking whether your questions, labels or presence could increase tension. Safety covers staff, respondents and researchers: share itineraries, avoid risky routes, and have a referral plan. Reflexivity means noting how your position shapes the data.

sections.heading: Data quality and example
sections.text: Data quality depends on reliability (repeatable measures), validity (measuring what you claim) and, in qualitative work, trustworthiness: clear records, careful coding and checking with participants. Keep field notes, recordings and a decision trail. In a hypothetical survey of 200 households, 150 completed interviews give a response rate of 150 ÷ 200 = 75%. If 90 of the 150 say they feel safe, that is 90 ÷ 150 = 60%. Report both figures: the first shows coverage, the second the finding. Do not present 60% as if all 200 answered.

keyPoints: Research design links a question to evidence and states sampling and limits.
Qualitative methods study meanings; quantitative methods measure variables; mixed methods combine them.
Informed consent, confidentiality and do no harm are basic ethical duties in conflict fieldwork.
Conflict sensitivity asks whether the research could worsen tensions; safety planning protects researchers and participants.
Data quality rests on reliability, validity and trustworthiness, supported by records and triangulation.
Response rate = completed interviews ÷ attempted sample × 100; subgroup percentage = subgroup ÷ valid responses × 100.

en.title: Professional Practice and Ethics in Peace Work
en.short: Covers neutrality, impartiality, confidentiality, do no harm, boundaries, burnout and accountability in peace work.

sections.heading: Neutrality and impartiality
sections.text: Neutrality means not siding with parties to a conflict. Impartiality means treating people according to need and without discrimination. They are related but not the same. A mediator may need neutrality to be trusted. A humanitarian worker may stay neutral in fighting while being impartial in aid. A human rights monitor is usually impartial about facts but not neutral about abuses. In mediation, neutrality concerns the process and the mediator’s conduct, not pretending that power is equal. Impartiality requires giving each side a fair chance to speak. Organisations set their own rules, so check the code that applies.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and harm
sections.text: Confidentiality means keeping information shared in trust private. It builds trust, but it has limits. A worker may have to break confidentiality if there is a serious threat to life or if the law requires a report, after telling the person in advance where possible. Confidentiality rules vary by role, organisation and country. Do no harm means checking whether an action, even with good intent, could create new risks. Ask who gains, who may be endangered, and whether the community agrees. A well-meant project can raise tensions or expose people who speak to outsiders.

sections.heading: Boundaries and burnout
sections.text: Boundaries are clear limits on role, time and relationships. They protect both worker and community. A peace worker should not become a permanent provider, lend money, or counsel close relatives without referral. Boundaries also cover physical safety and online contact. Workers should refer cases beyond their competence. Burnout is long-term exhaustion from unrelieved work stress. Signs include cynicism, exhaustion and reduced effectiveness. Supervision, realistic workloads, rest and peer support help. Self-care is not a luxury; it protects judgement.

sections.heading: Accountability
sections.text: Accountability means being answerable for decisions to affected people, employers, funders and the law. It needs records, complaint channels and honest reporting. Case: Amina mediates a land dispute in a Nigerian town. A party privately offers her money. She refuses, records it and tells her supervisor.

keyPoints: Neutrality is not taking sides in a conflict; impartiality is treating people by need without discrimination.
Confidentiality builds trust but can be limited by serious risk or legal duty, and rules vary by role and country.
Do no harm means checking for unintended risks before and during an intervention.
Boundaries set clear limits on role, time and relationships, and workers should refer cases beyond their competence.
Burnout is long-term exhaustion from unrelieved work stress, and supervision, rest and realistic workloads help protect judgement.
Accountability means being answerable to affected people, employers, funders and the law through records, complaint channels and honest reporting.

en.title: African Peace and Security Architecture (APSA)
en.short: AU and regional communities, early warning, peace operations, norms and implementation gaps.
keywords: African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance

sections.heading: What APSA is
sections.text: The African Peace and Security Architecture (APSA) is the African Union’s framework for preventing, managing and resolving conflict. Its institutions are the Peace and Security Council (PSC), a 15-member decision-making body; the Panel of the Wise; the Continental Early Warning System (CEWS); the African Standby Force (ASF); and the Peace Fund. Regional Economic Communities (RECs) and Regional Mechanisms (RMs) are building blocks. The normative base includes the AU Constitutive Act of 2000, whose Article 4(h) allows intervention in grave circumstances, and the 2002 Protocol establishing the PSC.

sections.heading: Early warning and operations
sections.text: CEWS collects and analyses information on risks, drawing on REC systems such as ECOWARN in West Africa and CEWARN in IGAD. Early warning is meant to feed the PSC and lead to mediation, preventive diplomacy or deployment. The ASF is planned as five regional standby brigades for rapid peace operations. Missions have been ad hoc or hybrid: AMISOM in Somalia, later ATMIS and now AUSSOM, and UNAMID in Darfur. RECs also act: ECOWAS used ECOMOG in Liberia and Sierra Leone, and troops in The Gambia in 2017.

sections.heading: Norms and the Gambia case
