sections.text: APSA’s norms oppose unconstitutional changes of government and support democracy, as in the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance (2007). In The Gambia, after Yahya Jammeh refused to accept defeat in the December 2016 election, ECOWAS mediated and then deployed troops in January 2017 under Operation Restore Democracy. Jammeh left office and Adama Barrow took power. The case shows a REC acting first, with broad international support, an example of subsidiarity: action at the lowest effective level.

sections.heading: Implementation challenges
sections.text: Implementation is uneven. APSA depends heavily on external funding, especially for peace operations. Member states may lack political will or resist interference. AU and REC mandates can overlap, and coordination is slow. The ASF is not fully operational, and early warning often does not lead to timely action. These gaps mean APSA works best when a REC has capacity and local political backing, as ECOWAS did in The Gambia.

keyPoints: APSA links the AU PSC, Panel of the Wise, CEWS, ASF and Peace Fund with RECs and RMs.
The PSC is the AU’s 15-member decision-making body for peace and security.
CEWS and REC systems such as ECOWARN and CEWARN aim to turn early warning into early action.
The ASF is planned as five regional standby brigades but is not fully operational.
Norms include Article 4(h) of the AU Constitutive Act and the 2007 African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance.
Implementation is limited by funding dependence, weak political will, overlapping mandates and slow coordination.

en.title: Nigerian Conflicts and Peacebuilding
en.short: Communal, farmer-herder, insurgency and electoral conflict in Nigeria: actors, responses and peacebuilding challenges.

sections.heading: Conflict types
sections.text: Nigeria’s conflicts often overlap. Communal conflict is organised violence between communities over land, markets, chieftaincy or identity. Farmer-herder conflict is a communal conflict over grazing, water and routes, worsened by climate stress and rural insecurity. Insurgency is armed rebellion against the state; the Boko Haram insurgency in north-east Nigeria is the main example. Electoral conflict is violence linked to elections, such as thuggery, intimidation and disputes over results. These labels are not exclusive: electoral violence can have communal roots, and insurgency can exploit farmer-herder tensions.

sections.heading: Actors
sections.text: Actors include federal and state governments, the police and military, traditional rulers, religious leaders, civil society groups, youth associations, and international agencies. Their interests differ. Traditional and religious leaders often have local legitimacy but limited enforcement power. Security forces can stop violence but may deepen distrust if they are seen as partisan or abusive. Civil society groups can monitor, mediate and support victims.

sections.heading: Responses
sections.text: Responses range from military operations and police action to peace committees, dialogue, amnesty programmes and humanitarian aid. Nigeria’s Niger Delta amnesty is one negotiated response. State governments have also passed laws on open grazing, such as Benue State’s law, though enforcement and fairness remain contested. Early warning and local peace committees can help, but they need funding, data and coordination with formal authorities.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: Peacebuilding faces weak coordination, impunity, arms proliferation, displacement and deep distrust. Many responses are reactive and short-term. Durable peace needs local ownership and attention to land, jobs and governance. In Benue State, farmer-herder violence displaced communities, and the open grazing law was one response. The law addressed a real grievance, but it did not settle cattle routes, compensation or inter-group trust, so dialogue and monitoring remained necessary.

keyPoints: Nigerian conflicts often overlap; communal, farmer-herder, insurgency and electoral violence are common types.
Farmer-herder conflict is a communal conflict over grazing, water and routes, worsened by climate and insecurity.
Boko Haram’s insurgency in north-east Nigeria is the main example of armed rebellion against the state.
Actors include governments, security forces, traditional and religious leaders, civil society and international agencies.
Responses include military action, peace committees, dialogue, amnesty and humanitarian aid.
Peacebuilding challenges include weak coordination, impunity, arms proliferation, displacement and distrust.

en.title: Advanced Theories of Conflict and Peace
en.short: Structural, rationalist, constructivist, feminist, postcolonial and complexity accounts compared.

sections.heading: Six accounts
sections.text:
Structural theory explains conflict through unequal material and social relations and weak or exclusionary institutions. Rationalist theory treats actors as strategic calculators who choose violence or peace by expected costs, benefits and risks. Constructivist theory holds that identities, norms and beliefs shape interests, so conflict is socially made.

Feminist theory asks how gendered power, masculinities and women’s roles shape violence and peace. Postcolonial theory traces colonial borders, land regimes and knowledge hierarchies into present conflict. Complexity theory sees conflict as a nonlinear system with feedback, emergence and adaptation.

sections.heading: Assumptions compared
sections.text:
These accounts disagree about what drives action. Structural and rationalist theories stress material constraints and strategic choice. Constructivist, feminist and postcolonial theories stress meaning, identity and power.

Structural theory risks determinism. Rationalist theory risks a thin view of rationality that ignores culture and emotion. Constructivist and postcolonial theories can be hard to falsify. Feminist theory is often marginalised in mainstream analysis. Complexity theory can describe much but predict little.

sections.heading: Evidence and critique
sections.text:
Evidence differs by tradition. Structural claims use cross-national statistics, but correlation is not causation. Rationalist claims use formal models, experiments and bargaining data. Constructivist claims use process tracing and discourse analysis.

Feminist and postcolonial claims use qualitative, historical and participatory methods. Complexity claims use simulation and case comparison. A good critique asks what each theory can explain, what it leaves out, and whether its evidence could have counted against it.

sections.heading: Small case
sections.text:
Suppose a mine opens in a fictional district and protests follow. Amina and Chinedu join protests over water and jobs. Structural theory points to weak land rights. Rationalist theory points to leaders weighing repression and concessions. Constructivist theory points to narratives of exclusion.

Feminist theory notes that women fetch water but are absent from talks. Postcolonial theory points to colonial land law. Complexity theory shows protest, crackdown and migration feeding back. No single account is enough.

keyPoints: Structural theory links conflict to unequal relations and exclusionary institutions.
Rationalist theory explains choices through expected costs, benefits and risks.
Constructivist, feminist and postcolonial theories treat identities, gender and colonial history as causal.
Complexity theory stresses feedback, emergence and adaptation, so prediction is limited.
Each account has blind spots: determinism, thin rationality, weak falsifiability or poor prediction.
Strong analysis compares assumptions and evidence and combines accounts rather than choosing one.

en.title: Peacebuilding and Statebuilding Theory: Liberal, Local and Decolonial Debates
en.short: Liberal peace, local turn, hybridity, decolonial critique and statebuilding in theory and evaluation.

sections.heading: Liberal peace and statebuilding
sections.text: Liberal peace is the post-Cold War peacebuilding model that links peace to market democracy: elections, civil society, human rights, rule of law and security sector reform. Statebuilding is the related task of building legitimate authority, institutions and capacity, including a monopoly of legitimate force, taxation and public services. Roland Paris argues for institutionalisation before liberalisation, warning that early elections can harden divisions. Critics reply that the model exports a Western state form and underplays history and local legitimacy.

sections.heading: Local turn and hybridity
sections.text: The local turn treats local people as agents, not recipients. It studies customary justice, everyday peace and local norms, while warning against romanticising the local. Hybridity describes institutions and norms that mix international and local elements. Hybrid arrangements may gain legitimacy, but they can also entrench local elites. Consider a fictional district, Kiro. Donors fund a council and a women’s peace committee, while elders control land. A hybrid land panel includes both, yet elders dominate its agenda. Evaluation must ask who is heard, who is excluded and whether the mix protects rights.

sections.heading: Decolonial critique
sections.text: Decolonial critique sees liberal peace as carrying colonial continuities: Eurocentric knowledge, racialised hierarchies and outside definitions of order. It asks whose peace is being built and who defines the local. The implication is not to reject all international support, but to analyse history, sovereignty and power, and to make ownership real rather than token.

sections.heading: Practice and evaluation
sections.text: Practice should start from a theory of change, use conflict sensitivity and combine quantitative and qualitative evidence. Evaluation needs baselines, perception surveys and attention to unintended effects and attribution. It should judge statebuilding by legitimate institutions and rights protection, not only capacity or speed.

keyPoints: Liberal peace links peace to market democracy, rights and institutions; statebuilding builds legitimate authority and capacity.
Paris’s institutionalisation before liberalisation warns that early elections can harden divisions.
The local turn treats local actors as agents and cautions against romanticising the local.
Hybridity mixes international and local norms and institutions; it can build legitimacy or entrench elites.
Decolonial critique highlights colonial continuities, Eurocentrism and the politics of defining the local.
Evaluation should use theory of change, baselines, perception data and conflict sensitivity, and judge legitimacy and rights, not only outputs.

en.title: Research Methods and the Dissertation
en.short: Advanced research design, ethics and fieldwork, mixed methods, analysis and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Designing the study
sections.text:
A master’s dissertation starts with a research question that is narrow enough to answer with the time and access you have. The design is the plan that links question, concepts, evidence and analysis. In peace and conflict studies, a case study examines one conflict, process or institution in depth; a comparative design examines several cases using the same categories. State your unit of analysis, the thing you are studying, such as an organisation, a community or a peace agreement. Explain how you will operationalise key concepts, meaning how you turn an idea such as reconciliation into observable indicators. Your design should say what evidence would count against your argument.

A strong design also states its limits. If access to a conflict zone is unsafe, a document-based design may be more ethical and still answer a useful question.

sections.heading: Ethics and fieldwork
sections.text: Fieldwork means collecting data where the conflict or peace work happens. It raises risks that desk research does not. Informed consent means people understand the purpose, risks and uses of the study before agreeing. Do no harm means anticipating how questions, notes or publication could endanger participants. Anonymity protects identity; confidentiality protects what people say. In a northern Nigerian case, a student named Amina interviewing displaced women should seek local ethics approval, use interpreters, avoid recording names, and store files encrypted. Researchers must also plan for their own safety, not promise benefits they cannot deliver.

sections.heading: Mixed methods and analysis
sections.text: Mixed methods combine qualitative data, such as interviews and documents, with quantitative data, such as survey counts. Triangulation means checking a finding against more than one source or method. Qualitative analysis uses coding, labelling text passages to build themes; quantitative analysis may use descriptive statistics or regression, a method for estimating relationships between variables. Choose analysis to fit the question. Reflexivity means examining how your position shapes the data.

sections.heading: Writing the dissertation
sections.text: The dissertation is an argument. Structure it around chapters: introduction, literature review, methodology, findings, discussion and conclusion. The methodology chapter justifies design, sampling (how cases or people are selected), ethics and limits. Keep a record of decisions. Draft, revise for clarity, and cite sources accurately.

keyPoints: A dissertation design must link a narrow question to concepts, evidence and analysis.
Define the unit of analysis and operationalise concepts before fieldwork.
Informed consent, anonymity, confidentiality and do no harm are core ethical requirements.
Mixed methods combine qualitative and quantitative evidence; triangulation checks findings across sources.
Analysis must fit the research question, and reflexivity records the researcher’s influence.
The dissertation is a structured argument, and the methodology chapter justifies design, sampling, ethics and limits.

en.title: Peace Measurement and Impact Evaluation
en.short: Measuring peace, conflict and fragility; indices; causal impact evaluation; limits of metrics.

sections.heading: Measuring peace and conflict
sections.text: Measurement turns concepts into indicators: observable variables used as proxies for hard-to-see things such as violence, trust or state capacity. Conflict data include event counts from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) and Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), surveys and expert coding. Peace is often split into negative peace, the absence of violence, and positive peace, institutions and attitudes that sustain it. Reporting rules mean recorded events can rise without more fighting.

sections.heading: Indices and fragility
sections.text: An index combines indicators into one number. The Global Peace Index, Positive Peace Index and Fragile States Index are well-known examples; each selects indicators, normalises them and assigns weights. Rankings are useful for comparison and advocacy, but weights are judgements. A country can look peaceful because violence is hidden or data are missing. Fragility measures usually combine exposure to shocks, state legitimacy and capacity. Read the codebook and year.

sections.heading: Impact evaluation
sections.text: Impact evaluation asks whether an intervention caused a change. The counterfactual is what would have happened without it. Random assignment, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables and matching try to estimate this. Example: 50 villages receive a peace programme and 50 do not. Conflict incidents fall from 20 to 15 in treated villages and rise from 18 to 19 in controls. Difference-in-differences = (15 − 20) − (19 − 18) = −5 − 1 = −6. The estimate is six fewer incidents relative to the control trend, if the groups would otherwise have followed the same trend and spillovers are absent.

sections.heading: Limits and ethics
sections.text: Metrics are political. They decide what counts as peace, whose violence is visible and which programmes get funded. Good practice triangulates sources, reports uncertainty, protects respondents and avoids treating a score as reality. Indicators can create incentives to game numbers. Impact results are local and time-bound, so do not assume they transfer everywhere.

keyPoints: An indicator is a proxy; an index aggregates indicators with chosen normalisation and weights.
Negative peace is the absence of violence; positive peace includes institutions and attitudes that sustain it.
Difference-in-differences = (treated after − treated before) − (control after − control before).
Causal inference needs a credible counterfactual and assumptions such as parallel trends.
Event data reflect reporting and coding rules as well as actual violence.
Metrics have ethical and political limits; triangulate sources and report uncertainty.
